thread.title: Beijing's Dislike Sinks Xiaomi Valuation To At Best 30% Below IPO Price - Xiaomi (BATS:XI)

author: Ivan.Tang
title: Beijing's Dislike Sinks Xiaomi Valuation To At Best 30% Below IPO Price - Xiaomi (BATS:XI)
text:
Xiaomi’s ( XI ) bids for China and Hong Kong IPOs have suffered crippling blows in the last fortnight. It withdrew its Chinese IPO application, while its optimal valuation is estimated at 30% below its Hong Kong IPO price. Xiaomi’s nightmare started after its China IPO application was chastised by Beijing. A lack of official endorsement will continue to haunt Xiaomi.
The world’s fourth largest smartphone producer originally hoped to get the honour of “double first” envied by all Chinese unicorns: being the first one listed in Hong Kong with dual-class share structure and the first one listed under the Chinese Depository Receipt (CDR) system similar to Wall Street’s American Depository Receipt (ADR).
Chinese IPO Withdrew; Hong Kong IPO Price Cut To Range Bottom But Xiaomi’s dream was shuttered by the following crippling blows:
1. On June 14, China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), the country’s securities watchdog, posted on its website the document “Feedback Opinions on Xiaomi Group’s application documents on its public issuance of depository receipts” . The “Feedback” document asks Xiaomi 84 searching questions on practically every minute detail of its application.
2. On June 18, the group decided to delay its CDR application until after its Hong Kong IPO, giving no possible date.
3. On June 19, market rumoured that Xiaomi had lowered its valuation target range to between $55 billion and $70 billion from an initial figure it had revealed to the market of as high as $100 billion earlier this year. It was also below the more recent floor price of $70 billion that the company and its advisers had informally used as guidance for investors.
4. On June 21, Xiaomi said it intended to price its Hong Kong IPO between HK$17 ($2.17) and HK$22 ($2.81) per share, raising capital between $4.7 billion and $6.1 billion, valuing the company at between $54 billion and $70 billion. Both figures will increase by 15% if over-allotment option is exercised.
5. On June 23, CEO Lei Jun (see photo) dropped his previous claim of Xiaomi being an internet service company. He re-positioned the company as the first of the “new species” of technology companies being a hardware maker making money from internet services.
Source: Sohu.com
6. On June 28, Xiaomi was reported to price its IPO at HK$17 per share—the lower end of its target range. The capital to be raised will be thus lowered to $4.7 billion while valuation dropped to $54 billion.
7. On July 6, the HK$17 IPO price was confirmed by Xiaomi.
8. On July 9, Xiaomi shares stumbled on their debut trading in Hong Kong, closed at HK$16.8 after slipping as low as HK$16 or nearly 6% below the IPO price.
Xiaomi Grilled On Positioning, Financial Performance And Market Research Data These events all happened after the Chinese securities watchdog issued the “Feedback” document which is highly critical of Xiaomi’s CDR IPO application. A look at the “Feedback” tells us what challenges Xiaomi faces in its two IPO applications.
Some of the 84 grilling questions are difficult to answer. In particular, the CSRC demands justifications for Xiaomi positioning itself as an internet company which normally deserves higher prices than a smartphone maker.
On Question #81 , the CSRC points out that Xiaomi’s smartphone sales amounted to 53.715 billion yuan, 48.764 billion yuan and 80.564 billion yuan respectively during the three years (2015, 2016 and 2017) covered by the application document, representing 80.4%, 71.26% and 70.28% respectively of the group’s total revenues.
Yet, Xiaomi’s revenues from internet service, mainly from advertisements and mobile games, representing only 4.8%, 9.6% and 8.6% respectively of the group’s total revenues in that period.
“The issuer is asked to indicate whether it is correct to position itself as an internet company--not a hardware company--at this stage, by a comprehensive view of the company's main products, the exact nature of business, revenue composition and sources of profits.”
The commission also questions Xiaomi’s sources of clients in the next question. Xiaomi claims itself as a technology startup using hardware sales to stimulate internet traffic while using internet services to get income.
“By combining the company’s (existing) way of getting clients through internet, would the issuer (Xiaomi) illustrate if it can get clients by internet methods other than from (selling) hardware? Please also illustrate the future trend of internet monetisation, room for business growth as well as if (the issuer) has the ability of sustainable growth, based on the growth trend and penetration rate of smartphone market in China.”
The rationality of Xiaomi’s financial performance is also questioned. On question #83 , the CSRC points out that Xiaomi’s revenues were overall stable in 2015 and 2016 but rose sharply in 2017. During these three years, its gross profit margin improved significantly year by year. Yet its inventory and account receivables also jumped sharply, far exceeding the growth rate of revenue. “Please ask the issuer to explain the reasons and the rationality (of such discrepancy).”
Elsewhere, Xiaomi quotes extensively in its prospectus the market information and data from an iResearch report. On question #41 , the commission questions the credibility of the report. “The sponsors and lawyers are asked to check whether the report is customised for the issuer's listing; whether it is a paid report; whether it is a public report. Please advise on its objectivity and impartiality!”
Worst of all, the commission shows undisguised dislike of Xiaomi’s IPO application. Question #39 says: “Regarding the content presentation of the prospectus, the issuer is asked to use an objective and plain language for descriptions in the prospectus; to remove those languages and expressions that are propagandist, exaggerating and flattery.”
Observations: Xiaomi To Be Haunted By CSRC Comments In Next Two Years In view of CSRC’s 84 grilling questions, it is easy to have following observations:
1. To answer all 84 questions thoroughly, Xiaomi has to prepare hundreds, if not thousands, of pages of documents. The task takes months to complete and hence impossible to meet the double listing deadline.
2. As the CSRC has deep reservation on Xiaomi’s positioning as an internet company, the company faces a huge challenge to present an explanation the securities watchdog may consider satisfactory. It takes time to change its sources of sales, profits and users in order to convince the watchdog that its positioning as an internet company is appropriate.
3. It takes at least a couple of years before Xiaomi present a set of new three-year financial data the CSRC may consider rational. Similarly, the company might have to work hard for some years towards the goal of becoming an internet company before it can quote a public market report the watchdog regards as impartial.
4. Xiaomi’s most important task is to improve its business performance and prepare a new IPO application in order to give the CSRC a better impression.
Xiaomi Asks For Too Much By Positioning Itself As Internet Company The CSRC’s doubts and dislikes boil down to two related figures—the amount Xiaomi wants to raise in its Chinese IPO and the company’s valuation. The securities watchdog might have considered Xiaomi asking for too much.
Take two recent IPOs as examples. Foxconn Industrial Internet, a subsidiary of Apple’s (NASDAQ: AAPL ) top contractor Foxconn, started listing at Shanghai stock exchange on June 8 after a successful 27.2 billion yuan IPO, facing no objection from the CSRC. Previously, market rumoured that Foxconn had considered moving part of its smartphone assembly lines to India.
In contrast, CATL, China’s largest car battery manufacturer, started trading in Shenzhen stock exchange on June 10. It had applied to raise 13 billion yuan in its IPO but only got 6.5 billion yuan.
Xiaomi has asked for over 30 billion yuan in its aborted Chinese IPO. In view of these two recent hot IPOs, Xiaomi might have really asked for too much.
The fact that the CSRC challenges Xiaomi’s positioning as an internet company effectively means the securities watchdog objects Xiaomi’s high valuation. When Xiaomi started its duo-IPO application process, market rumoured that the company looked for a valuation of well over $100 billion, apparently on assumption that the company was accepted as an internet company, not a smartphone manufacturer.
Xiaomi Valued At HK$7.5-12 Per Share: At Best 30% Below IPO Price Then how to get a more reasonable valuation of Xiaomi? As the company failed to get profit in the first quarter 2018, I evaluate the company from its revenue performance. Just as the CSRC questions, Xiaomi’s revenue performance has been erratic. Its year-on-year revenue inched up 2% in 2016 but jumped by 67% in 2017 and rocketed 87.8% in the first quarter of 2018.
To get an optimal valuation, I assume Xiaomi maintains the 87.8% growth rate for the whole 2018 and keeps its 11% EBIT margin of 2017. This gives a 17 billion yuan EBIT for 2018.
Since both Xiaomi and Apple ( AAPL ) are mainly smartphone makers with some internet business, I take Apple as a pricing standard for Xiaomi. With Apple’s EV/EBIT ratio at 13, I assume Xiaomi deserves a higher ratio of 15 in view of its higher growth rate. This translates to a valuation of only $38.2 billion on a per share value of HK$12, about 30% below its floor valuation of $54 billion and the HK$17 IPO price fixed by Xiaomi.
But that is the most optimistic valuation. Xiaomi’s business environment has been fast deteriorating in recent months due to two developments. The US ban on the sales of Huawei smartphones has signs of spreading to other Chinese technology products. The US-China trade war effective last Friday will further deteriorate the prospect of Chinese technology sales in the US. Smartphone sales of Xiaomi and other Chinese-brands in the US will be next to zero in the foreseeable future.
Worse still, the Chinese domestic smartphone market has shown signs of saturation. The two headwinds together means competition among Chinese smartphone makers will intensify - all of them have to fight hard to keep or increase their market shares in the stagnant or slowing domestic and foreign markets.
Hence, Xiaomi is unlikely to maintain its 87.8% first-quarter revenue growth rate for the whole year. A 50% annual growth rate would already be a remarkable achievement. With a lower growth forecast, Xiaomi does not deserve a price premium compared with Apple. Hence, a more realistic valuation based on an EV/EBIT ratio of 13 arrives at $23.83 billion or a per share value of HK$7.5, 56% below the IPO price.
Conclusion: Xiaomi’s Share Price Performance To Be Haunted By CSRC Questions The CSRC’s questions on Xiaomi’s China IPO application were no doubt the reasons behind the company’s application withdrawal as well as the repeated cuts in its Hong Kong IPO price and valuation. The company has to wait at least a couple of years before presenting a new set of business and financial data that are more acceptable for the Chinese securities watchdog.
Before that, investors will continue to ask Xiaomi the same questions, especially on the justifications of claiming itself as a internet company rather than a smartphone maker. There is a simple criterion on this: Xiaomi will be universally accepted as an internet company when any change in its smartphone sale figures no longer affects its share price. Obviously, Xiaomi is still far from reaching that milestone.
Hence, according to my estimation, Xiaomi now can only be best valued at $38.2 billion on a share value of HK$12. This is 30% below its HK$17 IPO price which in turn is already the bottom of the original HK$17-22 target range.
Yet, two headwinds are now developing. One is Washington’s virtual ban on the sales of all Chinese brand smartphones in the US. The other is a saturating domestic Chinese market. They together force Xiaomi and fellow Chinese smartphone makers to compete more fiercely in order to maintain or even enlarge their market shares in the domestic and overseas markets other than the US. That will inevitably cut Xiaomi’s revenue growth and profit margin. A more reasonable valuation hence should be as low as $23.83 billion or HK$7.5 per share —a whopping 56% below the IPO price.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
